seo.title: Karmic tail 21 22 10 compatibility: The World, The Fool and the Wheel
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 22 10 compatibility: the couple enters through The World, walks as The Fool and faces The Wheel of Fortune. Read through the Dostoevskys.

title: Karmic tail 21-22-10 in compatibility: zero on the wheel
short: A roulette wheel has one pocket that is neither red nor black: zero. The hero of Dostoevsky's The Gambler uses the word for himself: "What am I now? Zero. What may I be tomorrow?" The couple's karmic tail 21-22-10 is built like that wheel. The couple enters its shared task wanting a whole world for two (21, The World), walks it travelling light, in leaps and fresh starts from nothing (22, The Fool), and its main task is The Wheel of Fortune (10): learning to live through rises and falls, and seeing that "starting from zero" is just another pocket on the same wheel.

sections.h2: A novel in twenty-six days: how this couple began
paragraphs: In 1865 Dostoevsky, crushed by debt, signed a contract with the publisher Stellovsky that had a trap in it. If by 1 November 1866 he failed to deliver a new novel of at least twelve printer's sheets, Stellovsky could for nine years publish "for nothing, and as he pleases, everything I write". At the start of October 1866 the new novel did not exist.

On 4 October a stenographer came to him: twenty-year-old Anna Snitkina. On the very first evening, reading back what he had dictated, she reached the words "she came back from Roulettenburg", and Dostoevsky stopped her: he did not remember saying them. "The action takes place in a gambling town which I have called Roulettenburg," he explained, and the opening was later rewritten. The whole manuscript had that title too: Roulettenburg, the town of roulette. The title The Gambler came when the publisher demanded "some other, more Russian" name.

They finished the novel on 29 October, in twenty-six days. The next day Dostoevsky turned forty-five. In those weeks "we both entered into the lives of the heroes of the new novel", Anna Grigorievna remembered. She liked the grandmother and Mr Astley, but the hero himself she "could not forgive for his faint-heartedness and his passion for gambling". Dostoevsky was "entirely on the side of 'the gambler'" and insisted that a person can have a strong character and still not overcome a passion for roulette. She did not yet know she was arguing about her own future.

On 8 November he told her the plot of a new novel. An ageing artist, ill, in debt, alone, meets a young girl: "let us call her Anya". Could such a girl love him? Anna argued hotly that she could. Then he said: "Put yourself in her place for a moment. Imagine that this artist is me, that I have confessed my love to you and asked you to be my wife." And she answered: "I would answer that I love you and will love you all my life!"

That scene is the key to this whole article. Dostoevsky told a plot with two real people standing behind it, and Anna recognised herself in it. The three cards of the tail do the same: they tell a plot in which the couple one day recognises itself. And the novel they started with, about gambling, zero and the wheel, became their shared life in less than a year.

sections.h2: The World at the entry: a couple that starts from the finale
paragraphs: The World is the last card of the deck, the card of wholeness and completion. In the couple's tail it stands on the point "Entry to the task": what the two want together, their shared language. In Lisovskaya this point lies on the line of tasks, so the same wish that brought them together can, in time, start holding them in place.

A couple with The World at the entry begins with the feeling that the main thing has already been found. The two quickly become "us": private words, a shared view of people, a plan for a big life (another city, a business of their own, the road), "so that everything is real". They want not a slice of the world but all of it, at once. The Dostoevskys literally began with a finale: the first thing they did together was finish a novel.

Two months after the wedding, in April 1867, they left for abroad, away from creditors and from relatives who pulled every rouble out of Dostoevsky. To pay for the journey they pawned whatever they could: Anna's mother took "the gold things, the silver and the lottery bonds" to the pawnbroker. In Russian those bonds are called "winning tickets", so even the escape into a whole world was paid for, among other things, with winning tickets. "We were going abroad for three months, and we came back to Russia more than four years later," Anna Grigorievna writes. Berlin, Dresden, Baden-Baden, Geneva, Vevey, Milan, Florence, Prague and Dresden again. In Waite's list of divinatory meanings The World has "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place", and reversed, "inertia, fixity, stagnation". The Dostoevskys lived both halves of the list: the road, and the years when the hope of going home "now appeared, now vanished".

The World at the entry has a reverse side: a world for two closes easily. Abroad, Dostoevsky kept saying that he was "done for", that he was "ceasing to remember and understand Russia", and both found it "unbearable to live in a foreign land". The Gambler puts it more harshly. Alexei Ivanovich admits: "I passed through Dresden and cannot remember what Dresden was like." And Mr Astley tells him straight: "your dreams, your present, most urgent desires go no further than pair and impair, rouge, noir". A whole world shrinks to the size of a gaming table.

In a modern couple this looks perfectly peaceful. Evenings only for two, friends dropping away one by one, a shared opinion of everyone else, delivered from above. The quarrels are not about the matter at hand but about whose picture of the world is right, and each one pulls the shared world towards themselves. Among the minuses of The World, Lisovskaya names isolation and "Groundhog Day". From outside such a couple can look ideal, while inside it lives in a hotel nobody has left in a long time.

The entry has one more trait: waiting for the final outcome. Walking into the gaming room for the first time, Alexei knows he "will not leave Roulettenburg like this": "something radical and final is bound to happen in my fate. It must be so, and so it will be." The World in its minus is the belief that somewhere ahead lies a final win, after which real life will at last begin. Wen writes of The World reversed: "Triumph and supreme greatness will come, but are delayed." The delay is the trap: while you wait for the final outcome, you live in a rough draft.

Anna Grigorievna named the strategy of such an entry in one sentence. Of the weeks in Baden she writes: "The only way to fight it is flight." Flight did rescue them more than once. But the main task of the tail was not solved by flight.

sections.h2: The Fool in the middle: the zero you start again from
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya the middle of the couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an "addition" to the main task. In our reading the middle is how the couple lives the way from its wish to its task. Here stands The Fool, a card with no fixed number: 0 in Waite, 22 in the matrix.

Roulette has its own card with no number. The grandmother in The Gambler, sitting down at the table for the first time, asks why the croupier swept up everything on the table after "zero". Alexei explains: "Zero, grandmother, is the bank's profit." Whoever bets on zero and wins is paid thirty-five times the stake. "Thirty-six chances against, grandmother." She bets on zero at once, wins once, twice, and from that minute she cannot tear herself away from it.

Zero is the most tempting pocket on the wheel because it promises everything at once. In the last chapter Alexei sums up his life like this: "What am I now? Zero. What may I be tomorrow? Tomorrow I may rise from the dead and begin to live again!" For him zero is not failure but freedom: from zero you can become anyone. That is The Fool in the middle of the tail: the couple goes through its task by way of new starts.

In its plus this is the best thing such a couple has. They are not frightened when the ground goes from under their feet. They can begin again in another city, in another job, with an empty account, and not reproach each other. A gap in age and position does not get in their way: Dostoevsky was forty-five, Anna twenty, and on the day of the proposal he laughed at her dreams: "Oh, you child, you child!" Two like this resemble best friends on the road: they laugh at failures, give more than they can afford, and always leave the other a little air.

In its minus it is the same thing, only without the ground. Every time things get hard, the couple has its answer ready: start over. A new city instead of a conversation, a new project instead of sorting out the old one, "starting Monday" instead of today. They start easily and stumble as soon as it comes to serious steps. Sometimes they seem to be a couple yet live like neighbours, and neither can say what they are to each other.

Baden-Baden, summer 1867, five weeks. Rereading her shorthand diary later, Anna Grigorievna called them "something nightmarish". Within a week the cash was lost and the pawning began. Once Dostoevsky brought home a purse in which she counted two hundred and twelve friedrichs d'or, and within two or three hours, coming back for them twenty coins at a time, he lost the lot. "Letters were written to my mother, remittances were awaited with longing, and that same day or the next they went on the game." Her wedding present, a brooch and earrings, was never redeemed. Every day in Baden began from a new zero.

But the same chapter holds something else. Between losses they went walking: "My husband and I covered many dozens of versts in the countryside around Baden." Away from the gaming room his "kind, good-natured mood" came back, and they talked for hours about everything. That too is The Fool: travelling light, two people and a conversation. The middle of the tail does not decide for the couple which of the two zeros becomes its life: the gaming table or the road.

paragraphs.h3: A clue: The Emperor hidden inside The Fool

paragraphs: Here the clue comes from the engine's arithmetic. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail comes from the two outer numbers: 21 + 10 = 31, and 3 + 1 = 4, The Emperor. For a couple the middle is added up differently, from the two partners' middles, and the result is 22. But add up the digits of The Fool itself, 2 + 2, and you get the same four. The Emperor has not gone anywhere. He is folded up inside The Fool.

The Emperor is order, walls, rules, the master of the house. A couple with this tail does not receive him ready-made. Dostoevsky described this choice to the letter. His Alexei shouts in an argument with the General and the Frenchman: "I would rather spend my whole life wandering in a Kirghiz tent than bow down to the German idol." Which idol? "The German way of piling up wealth." And he sketches a German Vater who hoards gulden while his son and the son's bride grow old waiting for their wedding, until twenty years later "the eldest himself turns into a virtuous Vater, and the same story starts all over again".

The funny thing is that both of Alexei's choices are wheels. The Vater turns a slow one: generation after generation, the same thing. Roulette turns a fast one: "to get rich all at once, in two hours, without working". A couple with The Fool in the middle easily runs from the first wheel straight onto the second. Its task is to find a third way: an order of its own, unfolded out of its own freedom, not borrowed from the Vater.

sections.h2: The Wheel of Fortune as the main task: "tomorrow" and "now"
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is the "Main task". Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the minus: what is not working for the couple and what it has to learn. Here stands The Wheel of Fortune. And the French word roulette simply means "little wheel".

In Lisovskaya The Wheel is the card of cycles: rises and crises come to a couple in turn, and the thing to work on is not the change itself but the way the couple lives through it. In the minus the picture is familiar. The couple lives in stripes: feast and famine, close and distant, silence and a row. Money arrives in a rush and leaves in a rush. Being together is hard, yet something holds them. And every time it seems the next turn (a move, a new job, a big contract) will finally even everything out.

This is the gambler's creed, and Alexei says it word for word: "one turn of the wheel and everything changes". The trouble is not that the wheel turns. The trouble is the bet on a single turn that will settle everything. Mr Astley answers him with a sentence that sums up The Wheel in its minus better than anything: "You will still be here ten years from now… on this very bench." A circle with no way out: the same table, the same bench, the same "tomorrow".

The Wheel's second habit in its minus is looking for someone to blame for the turn. The grandmother bets on zero for a long time, then drops it: "Throw that nasty little zero to the devil," and puts four thousand gulden on red. Zero comes up. "It's you! It's all you! You talked me out of it." Alexei replies: "how can I answer for all the chances?", and a minute later the grandmother is already pleading: "Fool! Stay, do stay… I'm the fool myself!" Accusation and reconciliation within a minute: this is how, in Lisovskaya, The Wheel's swings look when people blame fate and each other.

Anna Grigorievna put it more precisely than anyone. Of Baden she writes: "I accepted with great composure these 'blows of fate' which we inflicted on ourselves of our own free will." The whole Wheel is in that one sentence. "Blows of fate" are in quotation marks, because fate has nothing to do with it. And "we", although only he gambled. Waite wrote that behind the symbol of The Wheel lies "the denial of chance"; Anna understood that at the gaming table. A couple's turns are not the weather. Two people spin them, and only the two of them can sort them out.

Dostoevsky had his own answer to The Wheel, and it was right. In 1863, after Wiesbaden, he wrote to his sister-in-law that he knew the secret of winning: "it is terribly stupid and simple and consists in holding oneself back every minute, whatever the phases of the game, and not getting heated". This is almost Waite's "stability amidst movement". But the same letter holds a sentence more important than the secret: "However clever a man may be, with the most iron of characters, he will still break loose." Knowing that balance is needed is not enough. Iron will not hold it.

The ending came in the spring of 1871. The Dostoevskys had been abroad for four years, money was short, the return home hung by a thread, and he was sure he was "done for" as a writer. Anna herself brought up roulette: "why shouldn't he try his luck once more". He went to Wiesbaden for a week, lost, and wrote her a letter she would later quote in her Reminiscences: "A great thing has happened to me: the vile fantasy that has tormented me for almost ten years has vanished… Now it is all over! This was absolutely the last time."

She did not believe it: there had been many promises. But it really was the last time. On his trips abroad in 1874, 1875, 1876 and 1879, she writes, he "never once thought of going to a gambling town".

Put two sentences side by side. The last line of The Gambler: "Tomorrow, tomorrow it will all be over!" The letter from Wiesbaden: "Now it is all over!" Between "tomorrow" and "now" lies the whole main task of the tail 21-22-10. The gambler lives in the wheel's next turn. A couple that has solved its task lives in the present one. As for the ten years in the letter and Mr Astley's ten years next to the number of The Wheel, that is simply a coincidence, if a pretty one.

And here The World from the entry comes back. Wen writes: "If the card appears in the Seeker's present, it indicates contentment with the present." The whole world the couple dreamed of at the entry cannot be won tomorrow. It can only be held now.

sections.h2: Strength at the centre: the axle the wheel turns on
paragraphs: In every couple with the tail 21-22-10, without exception, the centre of the chart holds 11, Strength. The couple's centre is its shared atmosphere: what lies between the two and is not put on display. A wheel always turns on an axle, and for these couples the axle is always the same.

Strength is not a fist. Wen writes that this card is a reminder: "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." That is exactly what the "iron character" of the 1863 letter lacked. Alexei in The Gambler is sure that salvation lies precisely in character: "I need only hold out once, show character just once, and in one hour I can change my whole fate! Character is the main thing." Character, as he understands it, is the iron with which a wheel is held by force. Strength holds differently.

How, exactly, can be seen in Anna Grigorievna. In Baden she "never reproached my husband for a loss, never quarrelled with him over it". When he sobbed and begged forgiveness, she looked for a way out and took him for a walk or to read the newspapers. She did not become his warder, so he had no one to hide from. And in 1871 it was she who suggested the very trip after which the "fantasy" ended.

This is not a recipe, still less advice to pay for someone else's gambling. Anna writes that she did not count on a win for a minute and had long stopped believing his vows. What matters is the atmosphere, not the sum: at the centre of this couple there was no war over who was right, so the wheel turned on a calm axle rather than on a quarrel.

In Lisovskaya, Strength in a couple's atmosphere is when the two sense finely what the other needs, and tension goes into passion rather than into a fight. In the minus the same energy turns into a fight for leadership: each has their own truth, and each tries to break the other. For the tail 21-22-10 this is the decisive fork. If there is a fight at the centre, every turn of the wheel becomes a trial: who talked whom into the move, who spent the money, who talked whom out of betting on red. If Strength is in its plus at the centre, turns stay turns.

In the Dostoevskys' story he was the "gambler" and she held the axle. In other couples it is the other way round, or by turns. The cards do not hand out roles by gender: the centre is shared, and either of the two can hold it.

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: a deck that closes into a wheel
paragraphs: This section is about the drawings of Waite and Pamela Colman Smith, not about the cards on our site. They show what the numbers only hint at.

**The Fool at the edge.** Waite describes a young man who "pauses at the brink of a precipice among the great heights of the world". The drop holds no terror for him: "it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him, if it came about that he leaped from the height." The Gambler has a precipice of its own. Alexei swears to Polina that at her first word he will throw himself down from the Schlangenberg, the fashionable lookout on the mountain, "and it is a thousand feet there, I believe", she reminds him. And she gives the coldest reply in the novel: "Why should I make you jump off the Schlangenberg? It would be of no use to me whatever." The Fool's leap is worth something when it leads somewhere. A leap for show is only a leap. In German, Schlangenberg means "Snake Mountain", and on Waite's Wheel the serpent Typhon slides down the rim: one more coincidence that is hard to miss.

**Strength and the chain of flowers.** On the Strength card the woman leads the lion not on iron: in Waite's words, "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers". The lion, he writes, "signifies the passions". And he adds a sentence that argues with Alexei Ivanovich: the card "has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense". Not an iron character but a chain of flowers. Waite uses the same "chain of flowers" in describing The World: that is what he calls the oval garland in which the figure dances. For these couples the entry of the tail and the centre of the chart are tied by one garland. Looking at the same lion, Wen recalls a verse from the First Letter of Peter: "Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour." So the lion of Strength at the centre and The Devil, which stands in the values of most such couples, meet in a single verse.

**TARO is ROTA.** On the rim of The Wheel, Waite set the letters TARO so that they read ROTA, Latin for "wheel". Elsewhere in the book he agrees with the author of a manual of cartomancy who treated the whole deck, "from beginning to end as the Wheel of Fortune": Waite has "no objection to such an inclusive though conventional description". Wen calls The Wheel "the mandala of the tarot, encompassing the whole of the teachings in the Major Arcana".

Now the tail reads as a whole. The World is the last card of the deck. The Fool is a card with no fixed place: Waite gives it zero but discusses it between Judgement and The World, while "other systems", as Wen writes, "assign '22' to the card and place it behind Key 21: The World". Wherever The Fool stands, it stands right next to The World. In the first part of his book, listing the trumps, Waite even puts The Fool as item twenty-one and The World as item twenty-two: these are numbers of list entries, not of cards, but they are the couple's numbers, only reversed. The tail 21-22-10 runs exactly through the seam where the end of the deck becomes its beginning again, and comes up against the card that is the very name of that circle. The tail's hidden plot is written into the deck itself: after completion comes zero, and after zero, a new turn.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a chain or a choice
paragraphs: The couple's values, its spiritual purpose, come in two kinds for these couples: 15, The Devil, in 56.6%, and 6, The Lovers, in 43.4%. This is one more answer to the question of why the two met.

**The Devil** in the values is the question of what keeps the couple on a chain. The Dostoevskys named that chain in their own words. Anna on Baden: something "that would not let him out of its heavy chains". He himself, from Wiesbaden: "my hands are untied now; I was bound by gambling". And in a letter quoted by the editors of the Reminiscences: "No, now I am yours, undividedly yours, all yours. Until now I belonged half to this cursed fantasy." Lisovskaya's closing thought on The Devil in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. For a couple with this tail The Devil rarely looks like a vice. More often it is the dream of a win in the broad sense: a plan that is supposed to pay for everything, money that is about to arrive, a passion that has been given half a life. The value here is to name your chain out loud. Whoever belongs half to a "fantasy" does not fully belong either to themselves or to the other. There is also some arithmetic without any mysticism: all the numbers on a roulette wheel, from 0 to 36, add up to 666.

**The Lovers** in the values is the card of choice. Waite calls it "in all simplicity the card of human love" and writes that it "replaces ... the old card of marriage". For this couple choice matters because The World at the entry promises "once and for all", while The Wheel in the task reminds it that "for ever" is made of turns. Anna answered "I will love you all my life" to the plot of a novel, and then chose that answer again in Baden and in Wiesbaden. The Lovers in the values is not a vow made once but a choice at every turn.

sections.h2: How the tail 21-22-10 is formed: a worked example
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not calculated from one date. Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Take two dates: 02.01.1980 and 05.07.1975. The personal tail of the first is 9-3-21, of the second 12-19-7. Add them point by point:
The centre of this couple is 6 + 5 = 11, Strength. The couple's values are 6, The Lovers.
Running every date through the site's engine shows the example is not a fluke but the only way this tail is put together:

ul: the tail 21-22-10 occurs in roughly one couple in two hundred (0.501%), 54th by frequency out of 97 couple tails;
in every such couple, without exception, one partner brings the personal tail 9-3-21 and the other 12-19-7;
in every such couple Strength stands at the centre;
the couple's values are The Devil (56.6%) or The Lovers (43.4%).

paragraphs: This shows what the three cards are made of. The World at the entry is The Hermit plus The Hanged Man: the sum of two ways of standing aside from the bustle, solitude and pause. Two people, each used to keeping a little to one side, together add up to a whole world. The Fool in the middle is The Empress plus The Sun, a full cup and a child's openness. The Wheel in the main task is The World plus The Chariot: one partner has The World as the main task of their personal tail, the other has The Chariot. What one of them walks towards all their life, the couple already holds at the entry, and its main task is the sum of the two personal ones.

The couple's middle is not recalculated from the outer numbers. In a personal matrix it would be 21 + 10 = 31 → 4, The Emperor, which is why nobody has 21-22-10 as a personal tail. There are no other couple tails made of the same three numbers in a different order either.

sections.h2: How to break the circle: what changes the script
paragraphs: The wheel cannot be stopped, and it does not need to be: every couple has its ups and downs. The tail's task is to stop betting on the turn and to hold the axle. This is what works.

ul: **Turn "tomorrow" into "now".** Every "once we move", "once the loan is paid off", "once the project takes off" becomes one thing to do this week. The Wheel in its minus lives in the future tense.

**Know your zero.** Every such couple has a favourite fresh start: a move, a new job, "starting Monday", a big purchase. Before the next one, ask each other: is this a decision or one more bet on a turn of the wheel?
**Do not put the turn on trial.** "You talked me out of it" is the grandmother's line at the roulette table. Say "we", as Anna Grigorievna did: a couple's turns are spun by two.

**Keep a ritual that does not depend on the phase.** For the Dostoevskys it was long walks between losses. Anything done in feast and in famine alike will do: a shared dinner without phones, a Sunday drive, shared work.

**Unfold your own Emperor.** An order the couple builds itself: a shared budget, a day's pause before any big decision, slow cycles instead of lurches. Not a Vater planning twenty years ahead, but a measure of your own.

**Do not seal off the world for two.** Abroad, the Dostoevskys were kept going by letters from family and friends ("our only consolation", Anna writes), and above all by Maikov's letters. A couple needs people who see it from outside and can say that the two are sitting on the same bench again.

paragraphs: If the roulette in a couple is not a metaphor (bets, debts and loans that can no longer be stopped), the conversation is not about cards but with a psychologist or a specialist in gambling addiction.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a couple that no longer bets on zero
paragraphs: In July 1871 the Dostoevskys returned to Petersburg with debts, with creditors and almost no money, starting quite literally from zero. It was the same Fool, only no longer at the gaming table. Early in 1873 the first book they published themselves came out: Demons. Three thousand copies sold by the end of the year. Customers got muddled over the title and asked the girl at the counter for "the enemy power" or for "ten or so of those 'devils'". That book began their joint publishing work, later hers alone, which lasted thirty-eight years.

The wheel turned the other way, but not by luck. A print run, the sales, the next print run: a circle too, only a slow one and their own. In Lisovskaya, The Wheel in its plus is a couple that changes its life together and pays its debts on time. The World in its plus is shared work: he wrote, she took it down, copied it out and published it. The Fool in its plus is the ability to start from zero without fear and without betting on that zero. Twelve years after the wedding Dostoevsky wrote to his wife: "you are my only sovereign lady, and this after 12 years!"

The first sentence Anna took down from Dostoevsky was a mistake: "she came back from Roulettenburg". Over four years later they really did come back from the town of roulette, both of them. That is the strong version of the tail 21-22-10: a couple that knows how to start from zero and no longer bets on it.

ul: **Entry to the task: 21, The World.** What the couple wants together: a whole world of its own, a big life with nothing petty in it, the open road, one shared view of everything. The same wish turns into resistance when the world for two closes itself off from everyone else.

**Middle of the task: 22, The Fool.** How the couple moves towards the task (our reading): travelling light, ready to drop everything and begin again. This is its courage, and also its habit of betting on a new start.

**Main task: 10, The Wheel of Fortune.** What the couple has to learn: to go through ups and downs together, to blame neither fate nor each other for the turns, and to keep its balance while the wheel spins.

intro: What follows is an investigation. The clues are in the cards themselves, in the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, and in the numbers from the site's engine. The key witness is a couple who lived these three cards in exactly this order: Fyodor Dostoevsky and Anna Snitkina. We have not calculated their matrix and do not claim this is their tail: the story was chosen not by dates but because its three cards stand where the couple's do. (Quotations from The Gambler, Anna Dostoevskaya's Reminiscences and Dostoevsky's letters are our own translations.)

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-22-10 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix, the task of the union. Entry to the task is The World: the two want a whole world for two. The middle is The Fool: they move towards the task through new beginnings. The main task is The Wheel of Fortune: learning to go through rises and falls together, not staking everything on one turn and not blaming each other for the turns.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 22 and not 4?
faq.a: Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices. The couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles: 3 + 19 = 22. The sum of the outer numbers, 21 + 10, would give 4, The Emperor, but that is not how the couple's middle is calculated. Even so, 2 + 2 is also 4: it is as if The Emperor were folded up inside The Fool.

faq.q: Can 21-22-10 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the reduced sum of the entry and the main task, and 21 + 10 reduces to 4. So 21-22-10 occurs only for couples, roughly one couple in two hundred.

faq.q: Is 21-22-10 a hard tail for a couple?
faq.a: A tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast. It describes a task: what may not be working for the couple and what it has to learn. The Wheel in the main task means there will be ups and downs; the question is how the couple lives through them, with an axle at the centre or with a bet on the next turn.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Running dates through the site's engine shows that 21, 22 and 10 form a couple's tail only in this order.

faq.q: Why an article about the Dostoevskys if their dates are different?
faq.a: We have not calculated their couple matrix and do not claim this is their tail. The story was chosen because its three cards come in the same order: an escape into a whole world, a life from zero, and a wheel that stopped once they stopped betting on it.

report: In Dostoevsky's The Gambler the hero sums up his life in two sentences: "one turn of the wheel and everything changes" and "What am I now? Zero. What may I be tomorrow?" The wheel and the zero are two of the three cards of the tail 21-22-10. The third, The World, is what the gambler stakes everything on: a whole life won in one go. A couple with this tail enters its shared task wanting a whole world for two, walks it through fresh starts from nothing, and its main task is The Wheel of Fortune. The tail's secret is that zero sits on the same wheel: "starting from zero" is just another of its pockets.

The best witnesses to this plot are Dostoevsky himself and Anna Snitkina. They met in October 1866, when in twenty-six days he dictated to her a novel whose manuscript was titled Roulettenburg, the town of roulette. A month later he proposed to her by telling the plot of a "new novel" about an ageing artist and a girl called Anya, and asking what she would answer in the girl's place. She replied that she loved him and would love him all her life. Within less than a year the novel about gambling, zero and the wheel had become their shared life.

report.h3: A whole world for two, and all at once

report: The World at the entry is the wish for everything at once. Such a couple quickly becomes "us": private words, a shared view of people, a plan for a big life where everything is real. The Dostoevskys went abroad "for three months" and came back more than four years later. The reverse side of The World is a world for two that closes itself off: friends drop away one by one, and the dreams of the hero of The Gambler shrink to "pair and impair, rouge, noir". And there is the waiting for the final outcome: somewhere ahead lies a final win, after which real life will begin. While the couple waits for it, it lives in a rough draft.

"Zero, grandmother, is the bank's profit," the hero of the novel explains. "Thirty-six chances against." Yet zero tempts more than any other pocket, because it promises a fresh start: "Tomorrow I may rise from the dead and begin to live again!" The Fool in the middle of the tail is how the couple walks the way: travelling light, ready to drop everything and begin again. In its plus this is a rare gift. They are not frightened when the ground goes from under their feet; they can start with an empty account and not reproach each other. In its minus every difficulty gets the same answer: a new start. A new city instead of a conversation, a new project instead of sorting out the old one, "starting Monday" instead of today.

In the summer of 1867 in Baden-Baden every day of the Dostoevskys began from a new zero: a loss, the pawnshop, letters to Anna's mother, and money that went on the game that same day or the next. But between losses they went walking for dozens of versts and talked for hours about everything. The Fool offers a couple two zeros to choose from: the gaming table or the road.

report.h3: Blows of fate dealt by one's own hand

report: The Wheel in the main task is read through the minus. The couple lives in stripes (feast and famine, close and distant, silence and a row) and each time waits for the turn that will even everything out: a move, a new job, a big contract. The Wheel's second habit is looking for someone to blame. The grandmother in The Gambler abandons her zero, bets on red, and zero is exactly what comes up. She turns on her companion for talking her out of it, and a minute later cries: "I'm the fool myself!"

Anna Grigorievna said it more precisely about Baden. She accepted "these 'blows of fate' which we inflicted on ourselves of our own free will". Fate is in quotation marks because it has nothing to do with it. And "we", although only he gambled. **A couple's turns are spun by two, and only the two of them can sort them out.**

At the centre of the chart such couples always have Strength, the shared atmosphere inside the union. Dostoevsky knew the secret of the game as early as 1863: "holding oneself back every minute, whatever the phases of the game, and not getting heated". And in the same breath he admitted: "However clever a man may be, with the most iron of characters, he will still break loose." Strength does not hold with iron: Waite writes that the lion of this card "is being led by a chain of flowers". Anna never reproached her husband for a loss and never became his warder, and when he sobbed she took him out walking. This is not advice to pay for someone else's gambling but a description of an atmosphere: **at the centre of the couple there is no war over who is right**, and the wheel turns on a calm axle rather than on a quarrel. Either of the two can hold that axle.

The last line of The Gambler is "Tomorrow, tomorrow it will all be over!" In the spring of 1871, after his last trip to Wiesbaden, Dostoevsky wrote to his wife: "Now it is all over! This was absolutely the last time." And so it was: he never went to a gambling town again. **Between "tomorrow" and "now" lies the whole main task of the tail.** Wen writes that The World in the place of the present "indicates contentment with the present": the whole world from the entry cannot be won tomorrow; it can only be held now.
What changes this script for a couple:

ul: turning every "once we move", "once the project takes off" into one thing to do this week;
knowing its own zero, the favourite fresh start, and before the next one asking each other whether it is a decision or one more bet on a turn of the wheel;
saying "we" about the turns instead of pinning them on the other;
keeping a ritual that does not depend on the phase: a walk, a shared dinner, shared work.

report: The strong version of the tail shows in the same Dostoevskys. Back in Russia almost from zero, they published Demons themselves, and that book began a publishing life thirty-eight years long: a print run, the sales, the next print run, also a wheel, only a slow one and their own. **A couple with this tail knows how to start from zero, and no longer bets on it.**
If the roulette in a couple is not a metaphor (bets and debts that can no longer be stopped), the conversation is not about cards but with a psychologist or a specialist in gambling addiction.

unit.meaning: Your task is to stop betting on a new start and to hold a calm shared axle while the wheel of rises and falls turns.
